entries.decision: Base on AOSP tag android-17.0.0_r1 (CP2A.260605.016), zero-fork-first with our own device/zune and vendor/zune trees; plan one rebase onto the Q4-2026 AOSP drop before beta freeze.

keyPoints.text: Base is AOSP tag android-17.0.0_r1, build CP2A.260605.016, API 37, security patch level 2026-06-05; GrapheneOS and LineageOS 24.0 pin it.
Observed: AOSP source lands about Q2 and Q4. GrapheneOS had no AOSP rebase Jan-May 2026; QPR1 (Sep 2026) is not in AOSP.
A 49-commit batch including security fixes, authored Mar-Jul 2026, landed in GrapheneOS on 2026-09-09; median lag 127 days.
Android 15 security tags had 2-3 month gaps in 2025; mirror shows no Android 16 security branch five months after release.
AOSP carries a native supervision framework (SupervisionManager, Settings Supervision screen); three config hooks are empty for Zune's agent to fill.
Stock AOSP handheld products ship Browser2; CaptivePortalLogin and HTMLViewer are other web-rendering surfaces. Never inherit handheld_product.mk unchanged.
WebView source is undecided: AOSP prebuilt (freshness unchecked, no update path), own Chromium build, or licensed prebuilt.
Siso is the Android 17 default build tool; kernels still build separately with Bazel/Kleaf; Cuttlefish gives hardware-free CI (needs /dev/kvm).

entries.title: Clean minimal AOSP product configuration
entries.investorHeadline: Zune's OS image is designed as a default-deny allowlist, not subtracted from stock AOSP.
entries.decision: Compose Zune products from base_system.mk plus an explicit allowlist instead of stock phone products; enforce with a CI diff of the built image; overlays via RRO only.
entries.whyItMatters: A no-browser kids OS cannot let upstream components arrive silently; Android 17 already adds a Web App installer module. An allowlist makes drift a build failure.

keyPoints.text: Stock products cannot be subtracted: inherit-product leaves markers; no PRODUCT_PACKAGES_REMOVE exists. Only skipping the inherit, Soong overrides and built-in switches work.
Settings and the android package are prevent-disable; SystemUI throws if config_recentsComponent is empty. 3-button navigation lets a non-Quickstep Zune launcher work.
Many Mainline APEXes (wifi, bt, conscrypt, adservices) contribute boot jars and cannot be pruned by name; neuter via flags, feature masks, RRO.
AOSP's prebuilt WebView is not updated regularly (Chromium's own integrator guide); shipping WebView means a signed update path forever.
Neutering without deleting: unavailable-feature masks (Print, Credentials, NFC), static RRO overlays, config knobs, flags like RELEASE_WEBAPP_MODULE=false.
Guards: CI diff of upstream makefiles on each rebase; allowlist test over installed-files.txt; on-device checks: no http(s) VIEW handler, empty browser role.
Only platform-privileged apps (Home, Setup, Guard, Updater) are in-tree; other apps ship as SHA256-pinned signed prebuilts from Gradle CI.

AOSP's Supervision stack (SupervisionManager, config_systemSupervision) is a candidate parental-controls hook; maturity unknown. Enforcement model still open: platform role, Device Owner or ZuneGuard.

entries.title: Hardware target and device-support strategy
entries.investorHeadline: Pixel 10a/9a is the best-evidenced route to a relockable custom Android
entries.decision: Start on Pixel 10a/9a (D17), keep the product layer device-agnostic, and defer own hardware until volume and cash gates are met; Snapdragon is a later second source.
entries.whyItMatters: Device choice fixes the security story (relock with our own key), the patch burden, the legal exposure over Google binaries, and whether the child can ever unlock the phone.

keyPoints.text: Google no longer publishes Pixel device trees; builds use an AOSP tag, an adevtool-generated vendor module and Google's prebuilt 6.1 kernels.
Bring-up is tooling, not reverse engineering, but recurs every QPR: stock images lead the AOSP tag. Budget at least one platform engineer.
GrapheneOS ships Android 17 on Pixel 10a and 9a with its own verified-boot key: strong indirect evidence relock works. Own test pending.
The 10a and 9a share the zumapro platform but have separate vendor modules, kernel repos and QA matrices.
Pixel 11 is not ready: GrapheneOS excludes gen 11 from builds as '[temporary]', and lists no Pixel 11 as supported (2026-10-01).
GSI on any Treble phone is rejected: not redistributable, no community Android 17 GSI, relock likely fails on stock vendors.
With bootloader locked and OEM unlocking off, a bad image hard-bricks the phone; OTA needs A/B rollback tests and staged rollout first.
Reported: incumbents (Pinwheel, Bark, Gabb, Troomi) rebadge commodity phones and sell subscriptions; none builds hardware. Stock firmware plus policy is the fallback.

entries.title: Curated Snapdragon device set and BSP strategy
entries.investorHeadline: Snapdragon is a later tier: relock evidence is user reports only
entries.decision: Snapdragon is a later second-source/premium tier (D17), not v1. Qualify candidates on the Device Support Contract, a passing relock test and written OEM terms; Pixel stays v1.
entries.whyItMatters: Explains why most 'very high grade' Snapdragon phones are excluded or unproven on tamper-proofing, and what must be proven before a second-source or premium tier.

keyPoints.text: Gate on a Device Support Contract, not the SoC: custom-key relock, OEM-unlock disable, A/B, AIDL HALs, 8 GB+ RAM, written OEM permission.
No Snapdragon phone has passed the contract; relock evidence is user reports (avbroot #299), none for Fairphone 6/6+ or Nothing (4a) Pro.
Only the Pixel 10a has vendor-documented custom-key relock. Rejected: OnePlus 13/15 (bootloaders reject keys), Galaxy S25/S26 (no OEM unlock), Xiaomi class.
Shortlist as candidates pending bring-up: Fairphone Gen 6+ ($649), Nothing Phone (3) ($799), Nothing (4a) Pro ($499-599), Motorola Signature 27 (unshipped).

entries.title: No-browser lockdown: threat model and enforcement
entries.investorHeadline: No-browser is enforced in the locked image, not by deleting an app
entries.decision: Compile 'no browser' into a locked, verified image: user build, Zune AVB key, WebView caller gate, no http(s) handler, INTERNET allowlist. Policy only tunes it.
entries.whyItMatters: The product's core promise depends on it. Real kid-control bypasses are hidden-browser bugs, so the defensible claim is narrow: no browser app, no way to type a URL.

keyPoints.text: AOSP 17 is not browser-free: CarrierDefaultApp (disabled http/https wildcard handler, JS WebView), OsuLogin and HTMLViewer are escape hatches.
AOSP 17 ships no WebView implementation. Vanadium (hardened Chromium, GPL-2.0 patches) or an own Chromium build means owning a Chromium update pipeline.
WebView gate: system_server already sees caller UID, so a ~20-line allowlist restricts WebView to two Zune packages (feasibility inferred).
App-level origin allowlists leak: shouldInterceptRequest misses redirects, blob:, javascript: and assets; Network Security Config has no allowlist.
eBPF denies INTERNET at socket creation per app. Stage 1 grants it to about 8 packages; the EPUB reader gets none.
Always-on lockdown VPN ('Zune Guard') adds domain/SNI control but AOSP leaks, and ECH and QUIC blind SNI filters; deferred to Stage 2.
Embedded YouTube in the Videos WebView carries the one Medium residual risk: its UI is third-party code with links we cannot remove.
Physical access bounds everything: a recovery wipe cannot be blocked, but leaves an inert device until a parent re-pairs, not a browser.

entries.title: Parental-controls platform: portal, on-device enforcement, sync
entries.investorHeadline: Google's parental controls aren't in AOSP, so Zune builds engine, backend and portal.
entries.decision: Build ZuneGuardian, a system app that is Device Owner and holds the SYSTEM_SUPERVISION role, enforcing signed cloud policy locally. Device Owner is a one-way door awaiting founder approval.
entries.whyItMatters: Parent control is the core promise. With no Google services there is no Family Link, so control plane, tamper resistance and offline behaviour must be built in-house.

keyPoints.text: AOSP ships supervision plumbing (SupervisionService, role, bound app service) with all config hooks empty; consumer features and Family Link backend are Google's.
SYSTEM_SUPERVISION role is system-only and exclusive; grants SUSPEND_APPS, lock-task, time, safe-boot and factory-reset controls, but not WIPE_DATA, private DNS or VPN.
Platform policy is thin: only per-app ALLOWED/BLOCKED/TIME_LIMIT, and TIME_LIMIT suspends immediately (open TODO). Zune must own the schedule, contact and content engine.
Cloud is authority; device enforces signed JWS ES256 bundles locally. Past expiry plus 14-day grace, it falls to guardians and emergency only.
Sync is one persistent TLS WebSocket as a doorbell (policy.update, then HTTPS GET); polling and alarms as fallback. No FCM, no UnifiedPush.
Fail closed: all apps are system apps; a persistent-data-block claim lock survives recovery wipes, leaving wiped devices inert.
Pairing: portal shows a one-time QR plus 8-character code (10 min, single use) in a parent session; the device scans it.
Stack: Go, Postgres, Redis, per-family KMS envelope encryption, React PWA portal with passkeys; attestation is a signal, not the root of trust.

entries.title: Release engineering: signing, OTA, verified boot, anti-theft, build infra
entries.investorHeadline: Zune forks GrapheneOS's update and signing plumbing; keys never touch the build host.
entries.decision: Recommended: fork GrapheneOS's 1,377-line MIT Updater into ZuneUpdater (update_engine plus static CDN files); sign offline with Zune-owned keys, one AVB key per hardware model; roll forward only.
entries.whyItMatters: Signing-key custody and update delivery decide whether a bad build or leaked key can hurt children's phones, and how costly recovery is. Patch cadence is a standing people cost.

keyPoints.text: OTA: fork GrapheneOS's 1,377-line MIT Updater; static CDN files with ed25519-signed metadata. Rejected hawkBit and Mender: neither drives update_engine.
Keys: AOSP key set plus one RSA-4096 AVB key per model, generated air-gapped; two-person offline signing; CI holds only the metadata key.
AVB key rotation is effectively a recall: custom keys are set only while unlocked, and lock transitions wipe data and rollback indexes.
Roll forward only: update_engine's SPL guard needs green boot state; Zune's custom-key devices are yellow, so Zune enforces SPL monotonicity itself.
Patching is a named 0.5-1 FTE job: monthly SPL train, 72-hour hotfix lane. No GMS means Zune owns WebView and Mainline freshness.
Benchmark: GrapheneOS, a partner, cut 43 release tags in 260 days; non-partner patch lag was about 125 days (report 01).
Zune Activation Lock: Android 17 has FRP-secret primitives and no UI; the station sets a secret, escrowed server-side under per-family KMS.
Attestation is a signal, not a gate (expects our AVB key hash, locked, yellow). Whether Google's RKP serves non-GMS OSes is unverified.

entries.title: Curated learning video: legality, technology, alternatives
entries.investorHeadline: YouTube is a gated, killable add-on; Videos must work without it.
entries.decision: Conditional go: offline licensed content plus paid partners are the base; YouTube is an optional made-for-kids-only tier behind a kill switch, dropped if refused or silent at 8 weeks.
entries.whyItMatters: The founder's core video promise (D2, D3) rests on a platform that can revoke access at will and whose rules collide with our containment design. The fallback protects launch.

keyPoints.text: No third-party YouTube Kids API; the sanctioned route is the IFrame player in a WebView, which needs no Play Services.
Four YouTube rules collide with our containment: no overlays on the player, no disabling links, no ad blocking, no offline caching.
Every embedded video must be checked as Made-For-Kids (MFK); we publish MFK-only for ages up to 12 to avoid mislabel exposure.
D3 topic requests are answered from our own catalog index, not live YouTube search, which allows about 100 searches a day fleet-wide.
Tier 2: one isolated WebView page on our own HTTPS origin, one iframe, navigation blocked in our client, remote kill switch.
Tier 1 is offline and native: Media3 player with no WebView and no INTERNET permission; signed content packs; ~40 h starter pack.
Licence traps, non-commercial: Khan Academy (CC BY-NC-SA), TED/TED-Ed, PBS KIDS. Kolibri and Kiwix packs include Khan and TED.
Curation is the real cost, not hosting: ~1,500-video launch catalog needs about 45 editor-days single review, 80 with double review.

entries.investorHeadline: Kid apps built in-house on Compose: no store, no GMS, roughly 80 person-weeks (estimate)
entries.decision: Recommended: at most six OS-coupled components in-tree; every other app in a Gradle monorepo, separately signed, silently updated. Compose UI, Readium EPUB reader without INTERNET access.
entries.whyItMatters: Sets build cost, update path and attack surface for every on-device app. No store UI and few INTERNET holders leave fewer ways to break out or leak.

keyPoints.text: Two tiers: at most six OS-coupled components built in-tree with the platform key; every other app is Gradle-built, separately signed, silently updated.
One stack: Kotlin, Compose, in-house ZuneKit design system with three age-band profiles, Hilt, Room; minSdk and targetSdk both 37.
Launcher written from scratch in Compose (5 pw). Launcher3 forks need a rebase every Q2/Q4 drop; Lawnchair is based on Android 16.
EPUB: Readium Kotlin Toolkit 3.4.0 (BSD-3, WebView-based, reflowable and fixed-layout). KOReader, crengine, FBReader, Librera rejected as copyleft or proprietary.
Readium's EPUB navigator is a WebView that intercepts every navigation and serves resources in-process, making a no-INTERNET Reader plausible (inference).
Only Assistant, Walkie, Videos, Setup, Updater, ZuneComms and Guardian hold INTERNET; WebView exists only in Reader and Videos.
Google services replaced: Sentry SDK for crash reports, sherpa-onnx for TTS and speech (AOSP has none), LocationManager for location, bundled OFL fonts.
An egress lint fails CI on android.webkit.*, http(s) ACTION_VIEW or INTERNET outside the allowlist; Cuttlefish boots the image in CI.

entries.title: Walkie-talkie (push-to-talk) and safe kid-to-kid voice
entries.investorHeadline: Walkie-talkie designed as our own Opus relay, avoiding a third-party voice processor; untested.
entries.decision: Build push-to-talk as Opus frames over Zune's own authenticated WebSocket relay, cloud-only, with parent-visible metadata only in v1; LiveKit SFU is Plan B.
entries.whyItMatters: Push-to-talk carries children's voice, so transport choice sets privacy exposure (no third-party voice processor), per-kid cost and what parents can see. The report is an unbuilt design.

keyPoints.text: Transport: Opus frames over Zune's own authenticated WebSocket instead of a WebRTC SFU; half-duplex 1:1 speech needs no SFU, ICE or UDP.

entries.title: Kid messenger, 1:1 video calling and shared comms backbone
entries.investorHeadline: Kid messaging and video are designed around parent-approved contacts and parent-readable threads.
entries.decision: Build one first-party comms service (Go, WebSocket, Postgres) with a parent-approved contact graph; server-readable text-and-emoji messenger and LiveKit 1:1 video; no recording, no E2EE in Stage 1.
entries.whyItMatters: Cross-family contact is where child-safety risk concentrates; the report calls one breach of children's chats existential, so trust model and moderation limits decide viability.

keyPoints.text: One first-party comms service (Go, one WebSocket per device, Postgres, Redis); Matrix and Signal rejected, XMPP kept as the 'buy' fallback.
Parent-approved contact graph governs everything; cross-family links need both guardians via invite code. No phone matching, address-book upload or kid-searchable directory.
Messages are server-readable with per-family envelope encryption; both families' guardians read threads, kid is told. No E2EE in Stage 1.
Text-only, 500 characters, no links, images or GIFs; age-banded emoji allowlist; server rules block URLs, numbers, handles and flag bullying or secrecy.
Video on LiveKit SFU (Apache-2.0) at 360p/24 fps; server can end calls; locked-down tokens; no recording or covert listening in Stage 1.
Android 17 catch: privileged background start gives no while-in-use capability, so camera, mic and audio live in the visible call app.
No-GMS push: persistent socket in a privileged service, Doze-allowlisted; battery and NAT unmeasured, ntfy evidence argues against 30 s heartbeats.
Known gaps: live video unmoderated; rules-only text filters miss coded language; social engineering of parents is the main cross-family threat.

entries.investorHeadline: Flashing takes about 10 minutes; eligibility, phone locks and custody are the real work.
entries.decision: Run v1 as an in-person-first scripted service behind a hard eligibility gate, not a mini-factory: 4-phone stations, per-model signing keys, parent-authorised service-unlock, staged cohorts (now ~200 users per D21).

keyPoints.text: Unlock and lock each need a physical on-device confirmation and wipe; 'two presses' is Pixel-only (Fairphone adds unlock_critical). Cannot be scripted.

Pixel bootloader updates raise an anti-rollback counter; newer-than-bundle phones are blocked pre-unlock. Pixel 10a reportedly excluded from May 2026 increment.
Rotating the AVB key is a recall, not an OTA: each phone needs service-unlock, confirmation and wipe. Keep per-model keys.
With OEM unlocking off, a locked phone cannot be re-flashed over USB; a parent-authorised service-unlock must be built before second batch (G1).
Attestation proves lock state and key hash, but needs Google's remote key provisioning, is relayable, and omits the OEM-unlock toggle.
Relocked Snapdragon phones may fall to bootloader exploits (Qualcomm GBL, EDL); keep Pixel the only pilot platform until each model is assessed.
Factory-mode app that creates attested keys and disables OEM unlock is an unmodelled bypass surface unless provably one-way after hand-over.

entries.investorHeadline: India's child-data law has no clear exemption for parent-visible monitoring, Zune's core feature.
entries.decision: Run an invite-only, parent-contracted pilot through an Indian entity with India-region hosting, Rule 10 parent verification at the flash visit, purpose-limited monitoring and 112 plus SOS, after Indian counsel sign-off.
entries.whyItMatters: Rs 200 crore is the maximum penalty for breaching DPDP s.9 (children), and parent message review is the feature at legal risk. Indian counsel's opinion gates the pilot.

keyPoints.text: DPDP s.9(3) bans tracking or behavioural monitoring of children; the Fourth Schedule has no parental-control or messaging exemption.
Defensible reading: the parent is part of the Data Principal (s.2(j)(i)) and consents, so Zune is a conduit. Unsettled; counsel gate G1.
Child means under 18. Rule 10 verifies parents via held or provided details or a DigiLocker-type token; cards are not named.
Rule 12 never lifts s.9(2), which bars processing likely to harm a child's well-being; it bites on the AI assistant and messenger.
Dates: s.9 and Rule 10 bind 13 May 2027; MeitY floated 13 Nov 2026 (ungazetted). Behave as if in force now.
Reported, unverified: Centre will bar under-18 social-media accounts via IT Rules. Assume Zune's messenger is a social media intermediary; stay closed-contact.
POCSO ss.19-21: intermediaries lose s.79 safe harbour without reporting to Indian police; the person in charge risks up to one year.
Replacing the OS drops the vendor's triple-press SOS (2016 panic-button rules, unread); Zune rebuilds it and keeps a 112-only path (A9).

entries.investorHeadline: 200 Indian families are reachable; the INR 43-48k Pixel is the binding constraint.
entries.decision: Default: launch in Bengaluru, in person, four phases to ~200 families; Wi-Fi first, optional nano-SIM; telephony deny-all except 112; English UI; Pixel 9a/10a only; pricing unvalidated.
entries.whyItMatters: The funnel is the real risk: families must own or buy a Pixel at INR 43-48k, and unit economics at INR 399/month are thin once cloud cost is counted.

keyPoints.text: Pixel 10a: INR 49,999 launch, 47,999 now. The 39,999 sale price needs a bank offer plus exchange; budget INR 43-48k per unit.
Keep stock Telecom, IMS and CarrierSettings (Jio is VoLTE-only; 112 needs IMS) but deny everything except 112.
Platform emergency numbers come from the modem, so '112 always works' is unproven; enforce 112-only in Zune's screen and field-test per carrier.
Child's SIM is an ordinary KYC'd SIM in the parent's name; moved to another phone, it escapes all OS controls.
Language (D20): English UI; assistant understands Hinglish but replies in simple English; a 300-prompt Indian-English/Hinglish safety eval gates release.
Cell-broadcast alerts: keep CellBroadcastReceiver and Indic fonts; overlay link_method=none and enable_text_copy=false so alert URLs cannot become links (D1/D2).
Content: NCERT-aligned tags, never NCERT text; StoryWeaver (CC BY 4.0), ISRO, PhET, NASA; StoryWeaver bulk ingestion and ISRO rewrites need written permission.
Weather: Open-Meteo (USD 29/month) plus NDMA SACHET CAP feed and CPCB AQI; IMD API needs an agreement and a fixed-IP server proxy.

risks.risk: Funnel: INR 35-48k phone for a child; Pixel is small in India (about 2% of premium, weak source).
risks.mitigation: Waitlist page to test demand; refurbished after eligibility test; Pixel 8a only if price-sensitive.

risks.risk: Carrier behaviour on a custom OS (Jio IMS, SIM-less 112, Vi, BSNL) is untested.
risks.mitigation: Gate G0 carrier matrix before any family; promise no SIM-less 112 until tested.

risks.risk: Google firmware redistribution unanswered; blocks beyond about 100 devices.
risks.mitigation: Written Google answer gates phase C2; Indian counsel and Google outreach now.

risks.risk: DPDP parental visibility versus 'behavioural monitoring'; messenger may count as social media; Karnataka under-16 plan.
risks.mitigation: Run C0-C1 invite-only and free until counsel clears R19 gates G1-G10.

risks.risk: INR 199 founding price is below per-child cloud cost; courier price loses money past about INR 1,540 round trip.
risks.mitigation: Rework founding price; test pricing on the waitlist before charging; measure real cloud cost.

entries.stage1: Four staged phases from Bengaluru. Pre-flash checks: GST invoice, IMEI via Sanchar Saathi KYM (SMS 14422), reject grey and US-SKU units, OEM-unlock and bootloader reads, battery health, nano-SIM tray. 112-only Emergency screen with read-aloud helpline cards (child cannot dial them: 'tell a grown-up or press SOS'). Carrier matrix G0; English UI; SACHET plus Open-Meteo weather.
stage2: Hindi and regional languages: Indic IME and fonts, ASR/TTS (AI4Bharat), Devanagari and Hinglish evals, translated content
eSIM LPA and UPI AutoPay
IMD data agreement; NCERT permission
Nothing and Motorola India devices after relock tests; own hardware (R21)
School mode, exam-focus schedule, sibling profiles, parent-opted location (counsel: DPDP bars tracking children)
openItems: Confirm first city: Bengaluru default meets Karnataka's under-16 social-media announcement (6 Mar 2026); counsel to weigh.
Test 112 with and without SIM on Jio, Airtel, Vi, BSNL; verify whether any consumer data-only SIM exists.
Founder to confirm age range (A8); R20 proposes NEP stages, ages 6-14.
Reserve of 4-6 company-owned replacement phones is a narrow D15 exception; founder approval needed.
Reconcile pricing with R19: free invite-only first phase until payments, GST and DLT are ready.

competitors.approach: Kid-safe OS on standard Android phones, including a Pixel 9a variant. No browser, no social, no app store on the phone. Parent 'Caregiver Portal' controls contacts, apps, screen-time modes and location. Carrier-agnostic. Added a kid-safe AI chatbot (2023) and the 'Pinwheel Home' landline (Jul 2026).

competitors.weakness: This is the closest analogue to Zune's Pixel + custom-OS plan, so 'Pixel + no browser' is not a moat. Small and thinly funded. Depends on a US carrier SIM and Google's hardware. No India presence. Its device mix shows the cheap devices carry volume and the $599 Pixel is a niche.

Inc. 5000 #212 (2024). No Series A found. NB: 'Pinwheel' payroll API is a different company with a $20M Series A and $50M Series B.

competitors.name: Bark (Bark Phone and Bark parental control)
competitors.approach: Monitoring-based: Bark app scans messages and social media for risks; Bark Phone is a managed Android phone on a T-Mobile MVNO.
competitors.price: Bark Phone service $39/mo (talk, text, Wi-Fi) to $79/mo (unlimited data) + device $10/mo (24 mo) or Pro $25/mo; Bark Jr $5/mo; Bark Premium $14/mo.
competitors.weakness: Allows social apps and monitors them, which is the opposite philosophy to Zune's no-browser design. US carrier-bound, and monitoring invites teen pushback. Not in India.
competitors.source: Bark pricing as reported by AllAboutCookies/Timily; Fierce Network
competitors.funding: ~$66M: Series B $10M (Jul 2020), Series C $30M (Jun 2022, Kayne Anderson Growth Capital), secondary transaction Jan 2026; acquired uKnow and Router Limits (Pitchbook/Crunchbase via search).

competitors.name: Gabb
competitors.approach: 'Safe tech' phones and watches with no browser, social or app store, sold with Gabb's own (Verizon-network) plan; the largest brand in this niche.
competitors.price: Gabb Phone 4 $149.99, Phone 4 Pro $199.99 (TechCrunch Jul 2026: from ~$159.99); plans $19.99 or $24.99/mo; Gabb Watch 3 plan $9.99-16.99/mo.
competitors.weakness: Locked to a US carrier plan. Philosophy is close to Zune's (no browser) but with no AI assistant, curated learning video or portal-first design. Not in India.
competitors.source: Gabb pricing blog (via search summary); Dealroom; Inc. 5000
competitors.funding: ~$30.4M over 4 rounds (Dealroom): $3.0M AIM Ventura (Mar 2020), $14.0M (Apr 2021), $13.29M (Nov 2021). Revenue ~$148.7M in 2025 per Latka (unverified); 895% 3-yr growth (Inc. 5000 #494, 2024).

competitors.name: Troomi
competitors.approach: Samsung Galaxy A-series phones with the 'KidSmart OS' parental layer, sold with a Troomi wireless plan.
competitors.price: Samsung A17 5G $249.95 (or $6.94/mo); plans $24.95 (Do), $29.95 (Dream), $34.95 (Discover, adds browser and apps).
competitors.weakness: Small, US-only. Higher tiers add a browser and apps, which dilutes the safety pitch.
competitors.funding: ~$11.3M; last round ~$11M (Aug 2023, Springtide Ventures) per CB Insights/Tracxn. No acquisition found.

competitors.name: Freckle
competitors.approach: Purpose-built $199 kids' phone for ages 7-13 with a 3.1-inch screen and proprietary ClayOS: no browser, no app store, no social media, no YouTube. Calls and texts with approved contacts, location safe-zones, and outdoor 'quests' and a nature-guide AI.
competitors.weakness: Very new and unproven; hardware plus carrier dependency; US only. Its philosophy (no browser, no YouTube) mirrors Zune's, and it shows capital is flowing to the idea. Small screen limits camera, video and reading features.
competitors.funding: Backed by Alexis Ohanian's Seven Seven Six; amount undisclosed. Founder Sam Terris (ex-Nuggs).

competitors.name: HMD Fusion X1 with Xplora
competitors.approach: Teen/tween Android phone from HMD with Xplora's parental platform (remote access, school mode, location, SOS) on subscription.
competitors.price: EUR 269.99 / GBP 229 (~Rs 26,461 per a conversion in the source); Xplora Guardian from EUR 4.99/mo.
competitors.weakness: Parent-managed but still a general phone (apps, browser possible). Xplora scale: 476,000 subscriptions in 2025, +33%. Not sold in India as a kids product (the India 'HMD Fusion' is an unrelated modular phone at Rs 10,999-17,999).

competitors.name: Light Phone III and Wisephone II (Techless)
competitors.approach: Minimalist 'dumbphones' marketed to adults and teens for digital detox. Wisephone II is an Android phone with the WiseOS parental/limit layer.
competitors.price: Light Phone III $699 pre-order, $799 retail. Wisephone II $399 + $15/mo WiseOS.
competitors.weakness: Not child-specific. Indicates niche willingness to pay $400-800 for a restrictive phone, but at tiny scale: Techless reported $2.25M+ revenue and 58.5% margin on Wefunder.
competitors.funding: Light Phone funding is unreliable. A $12.7M figure appears in some listings; the $86M Series C and $100M Series D in the same listing look like another 'Light' company, so I excluded them.

competitors.name: Google Family Link / Apple Screen Time
competitors.approach: Free OS-level parental controls: app approval, screen-time limits, location. The default for most Indian families.
competitors.weakness: Layered on a full phone with browser and YouTube. Easy for kids to work around. Gives no kid-only communication, curated video or AI. It is, however, the price anchor: zero.

competitors.name: Qustodio
competitors.approach: Cross-platform parental control app (web filter, time limits, monitoring). Part of Qoria, now owned by Aura.
competitors.price: Basic $59.95/yr (5 devices); Complete $104.95/yr; India price blogs say ~Rs 4,500-5,500/yr (low confidence).
competitors.weakness: Software-only, so it cannot remove the browser or YouTube. Consumer ARR only ~US$21M after ~15 years.
competitors.funding: Acquired by Family Zone (now Qoria) in 2022 (funded by an A$42M raise, per ASX release). Qoria shares fell ~32-33% after its Feb 2026 result despite ~25% growth, then Aura acquired Qoria (completed 17 Jul 2026, ~A$0.317 per Qoria share).

competitors.name: Net Nanny / Kidslox / Aura Family
competitors.approach: Net Nanny and Kidslox are filter and time-limit apps. Aura bundles identity-theft protection and Circle-based kids controls into a family plan.
competitors.price: Net Nanny $39.99 (1 device) to $89.99/yr (20 devices); Kidslox $7.99/mo or $39.99/yr; Aura Family $32/mo ($384/yr).
competitors.weakness: Software add-ons, with no controlled OS. Aura's value is identity protection, so kids controls are a bundle feature.
competitors.funding: Aura: $200M Series F at ~$2.5B (Oct 2021); $140M Series G equity+debt at $1.6B (closed Mar 2025); $100M placement alongside the Qoria deal (Jul 2026); acquired Circle Media Labs in 2021.

competitors.name: Fully Kiosk Browser and generic Android kiosk/launcher apps (QuadNode, Kids Place, AirDroid, FlashGet, Findmykids)
competitors.approach: Do-it-yourself lockdown: pin an Android phone to a few apps. In India: QuadNode (Pune launcher), eKavach (Delhi), many Chinese-origin apps (Findmykids 82M installs, AirDroid Parental Control 20M, FlashGet Kids 19M per an Impulsec roundup).
competitors.price: Fully Kiosk PLUS: one-time EUR 8.90 / $10.99 per device. Most parental apps are freemium.
competitors.weakness: Technically easy to copy, which proves the moat must be content, communication, AI and portal, not the lock. No compliant child communication layer or curated content.

competitors.name: JioShield (new) / Jio Safety Shield on JioBharat and JioPhone Prima
competitors.approach: Jio's family-safety service (launched 26-29 Sep 2026): location, SOS and battery alerts; parent controls screen time, app installs, calls and messaging. Child installs the JioShield app on Android 10+ with an active Jio number (iOS 'shortly'); parent uses the JioThings app. Earlier 'Safety Shield' on JioBharat and Prima 2 feature phones: restricted numbers, distraction-free mode, location.
competitors.price: Rs 1,000/year; the 10th-anniversary offer gives 10 x Rs 100 recharge vouchers (on plans of Rs 399+ ) so Jio calls it effectively free. JioBharat Rs 999 list, Rs 699 in a 2024 Diwali offer (2026 price not verified); JioPhone Prima Rs 2,599; Prima 2 Rs 2,799.
competitors.weakness: Weakness is for Zune to exploit: it is a control layer on a normal phone, which keeps browser and YouTube. It also needs a Jio SIM. But it sets a national price anchor of about Rs 83/month, and Jio's distribution is unmatched.

competitors.name: India kids smartwatches and phones (imoo, boAt, Noise, Easyfone Star)
competitors.approach: 4G kids watches with calling, GPS and SOS (imoo Z1, boAt Wanderer, Noise Junior Explorer 2). Easyfone Star (eNovus) was an earlier Indian kids phone with call whitelist, no browsing, GPS and SOS, configured via a website (CareTouch).
competitors.price: imoo Z1 from Rs 9,490 (Rs 6,499 on one Amazon deal); boAt Wanderer Rs 4,999; Noise Junior Explorer 2 Rs 5,499; Fire-Boltt Rs 999-1,199 (adult Bluetooth-calling watches); Easyfone Star Rs 3,490.
competitors.weakness: Calls and location only, so no AI, learning video or messaging, and a small screen. Indian smartwatch volume is falling (-17.6% in 2025). Easyfone Star is old (about 2017; current status unknown), suggesting Indian kids-phone attempts have not become visible brands.

tailwinds.item: India: Supreme Court and Centre move to bar under-18 social-media accounts
tailwinds.detail: 28 Sep 2026: a bench headed by CJI Surya Kant asked the Centre to consider statutory rules (18-year minimum for independently holding accounts, age checks, parental consent), citing minors' lack of contractual capacity (Indian Contract Act s.11). Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said the IT Intermediary Rules will be amended to stop platforms letting under-18s open accounts. Only days old, so details may change. Earlier reports mention a three-tier 8-12/12-16/16-18 framework.

tailwinds.item: India: DPDP Act 2023 and DPDP Rules 2025
tailwinds.detail: A 'child' is under 18. Rules notified 13 Nov 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E)). Verifiable parental consent before processing children's data (Rule 10, DigiLocker-style verification); no tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted ads to children. Consent-manager registration opens 13 Nov 2026 and core obligations apply from 13 May 2027. This also binds Zune's own data handling.

29 Jan 2026: flags digital addiction as a public-health issue; recommends age-based limits on social media, stricter age verification, default-safe settings, and parent workshops on using parental-control tools.

tailwinds.item: India: Karnataka under-16 and Andhra Pradesh under-13 social-media bans announced
tailwinds.detail: 6 Mar 2026: Karnataka's CM announced an under-16 ban in the state budget; Andhra's CM announced an under-13 ban to be rolled out within ~90 days, with graded access for 13-16. Goa is studying similar curbs. Still announcements: legal experts question state competence and no enforcing law was found. Status as of Sep 2026 not confirmed.
Madurai Bench (S. Vijayakumar v. Union of India) suggested the Union explore an Australia-style under-16 framework and stressed parental-control tools at user level.

State-led, no national rule. Himachal Pradesh bans phones in all schools from 1 Mar 2026 (Rs 500 fine and confiscation); Delhi has an advisory; Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Kerala and Tripura are reported to restrict (list not independently verified).

Online Safety Amendment (Social Media Minimum Age) Act passed 28 Nov 2024; in force 10 Dec 2025. Platforms (YouTube, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, Snapchat, X, Reddit, Twitch, Threads, Kick) must take reasonable steps to keep out under-16s; fines up to A$49.5M; no penalty on families. WhatsApp, Messenger Kids, YouTube Kids and Google Classroom are outside the ban.

Malaysia: Online Safety Act 2025 in force 1 Jan 2026 with an under-16 social-media ban, enforcement from 1 Jun 2026. Indonesia: under-16 accounts on 'high-risk' platforms (including YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Roblox) deactivated from March 2026. New Zealand bill introduced; Denmark (under-15) and Spain (under-16) planned or proposed.

tailwinds.item: EU: KIDS Act proposal and Parliament resolution
tailwinds.detail: 17 Sep 2026: the European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act (COM(2026) 681): EU-wide minimum age of 15 for own social-media accounts, no social media under 13, mandatory age assurance, and safety-by-design duties for games, AI chatbots and companions. Under-13s may use child-friendly video-sharing via guardian-managed accounts, a model close to Zune's curated Videos. Earlier, on 26 Nov 2025 the Parliament voted 483-92 for a minimum age of 16 (non-binding). France: age-15 law targeted for Sept 2026.

Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 (in force 29 Apr 2026) amended the Online Safety Act to let ministers require services to restrict children's access. 15 Jun 2026: government announced an under-16 ban on selected platforms after a consultation with 116,211 responses (nine in ten parents backed a ban); expected in force Spring 2027; 15 Jul 2026: default midnight-6am curfews for 16-17s.

Texas (effective 1 Jan 2026; enjoined Dec 2025, then Fifth Circuit stayed the injunction; Supreme Court denied emergency applications on 6 Jul 2026). Utah (7 May 2026; litigation ongoing). Louisiana (1 Jul 2026). California AB 1043 Digital Age Assurance Act (1 Jan 2027). They push the OS and app-store layer to carry age and parental-consent signals, which favours a child-specific OS.
UNESCO GEM (Mar 2026): 114 education systems (58%) have a national school phone ban, up from 24% in Jun 2023 and 40% in early 2025.

tailwinds.item: Parent movements: Wait Until 8th and Smartphone Free Childhood
tailwinds.detail: Wait Until 8th (US): >155,000 parents signed (2026, unverified). Smartphone Free Childhood (UK, founded early 2024): a Parent Pact to delay smartphones to ~14 and social to 16; sources conflict (>165,000 families vs >350,000 parents) and it has chapters in 39 countries. An IFS working paper found fewer mental-health problems in English primary schools where at least 20% of families signed. No India chapter or Indian pledge found.

market.funnelFor200Users:
Short answer: the Indian pool of 'owns a qualifying Pixel AND has a child 8-14 AND wants this' is only thousands of families nationally in my base case, so ~200 is possible but only with targeted outreach, not organic discovery. Every step below is an estimate with stated assumptions. No source gives Pixel unit sales for India, or the share of such families who want a kid-only OS.

PATH A: the family already owns a Pixel (D16/D17 as written).
1. Pixels sold in India, Jan 2023-Sep 2026: base 1.6M (range 1.2-2.2M). Built from: 2023 = 0.25% overall share x ~145-150M market = ~0.37M; 2024 = ~0.19-0.43M annualised from 'Pixel 5%' of 6.5M narrow-premium units (the 5% is ambiguous); 2025 = IDC 152M x Counterpoint 14% ultra-premium share = 21.3M x Pixel 2% = ~0.43M; 2026 year to date ~0.5M (Q2 alone = 4% x (33.2M x 14-17%) = 0.19-0.23M, with the Pixel 10a on sale from 6 Mar 2026).
2. Still with the original owner and in use: x0.75 -> base 1.2M (0.9-1.65M).
3. Subset that fits D17's '9a/10a class' alone: a-series was 73% of Google's India shipments in 2023; assume 50-70% of 2025-26 units -> ~0.5M (0.4-0.7M). If the qualification program admits any relockable Pixel (7a onward, 10, 11), use the full 1.2M.
4. Household has a child aged 8-14: assume 25% (range 18-32%) for Pixel-owning affluent households (older parents, fewer children). Not sourced. Base 1.2M x 25% = 300k (low 162k, high 528k).
5. Wants a locked-down, no-browser, no-YouTube child device and accepts ~Rs 5,700 up front + ~Rs 1,250/month: assume 2% (range 0.5-5%). This is a guess. No Indian evidence exists, and JioShield (Rs 1,000/yr) and Family Link (free) are cheaper substitutes. Base 300k x 2% = ~6,000 (low ~810; high ~26,400).
6. 200 families = ~3.3% of the base pool, 25% of the low pool, 0.8% of the high pool. If the 9a/10a-only subset is used, divide the pool by roughly 2.4 (1.2M/0.5M); 200 then equals about 8% of the base pool.
7. Reach needed: owners cannot be listed. Assume 0.5% of reached Pixel-owner parents with an 8-14 child sign up (cold niche D2C; assumption) -> 200/0.005 = 40,000 such parents, i.e. ~13% of the 300k base pool (~160,000 Pixel owners, ~13% of all Indian Pixel owners). At 0.1% you would need 200,000, which exceeds what exists. Realistic only through concentrated channels: Pixel owner communities (Reddit, Telegram, Pixel India forums), school/parent groups in the top metros, and word of mouth within a few schools (which the messenger's network effect needs anyway).

PATH B: the parent buys a Pixel for the child (a realistic way to reach 200 without relying on prior owners).
- A Pixel 10a/9a costs Rs 49,999 list (street ~Rs 38,000-45,000 with offers). With Zune's ~Rs 5,680 + Rs 15,000/yr, year 1 is ~Rs 59,000-71,000 (~$610-730 at Rs 96.3/$).
- Pool: ~21.3M >INR 45k phones a year x 25% (child 8-14) = ~5.3M households a year (an upper bound; units overcount households and upgraders). At 0.05-0.1% intent (assumption; no data) that is ~2,650-5,300 households, so 200 = ~4-8%.
- Risk: this is a Rs 60-70k decision for a child's device versus Rs 1,000/yr JioShield or free Family Link. Also, if Zune sells or finances the Pixel, D15/D16 (customer-supplied phones) change; if the customer buys it themselves (Flipkart, Google Store, Croma, Reliance Digital), they do not.

Bottom line: expect to talk to tens of thousands of parents to sign ~200. The binding constraint is not Pixel supply; it is willingness to pay Rs 1,250/month. The 200-user phase is therefore best treated as a test of that price, which the market data above cannot answer. Sensitivity: Pixel's India share is small (2% to 4% of ultra-premium) but growing quickly; the memory-chip shortage is lifting phone prices (Pixel 11 starts at Rs 89,999 vs Rs 79,999 for the Pixel 10, +12.5%).
insights: Analyst 'market size' numbers are not investor-grade. Parental-control software for 2025 ranges $1.57B-$2.8B, kids smartwatches $2.65B-$8.3B, children's smartphones $1.49B-$40.9B, and one vendor lists India's kids smartwatch market as '213.86 Billion USD'. Real company data is far smaller: Qustodio's consumer ARR is ~US$21M after ~15 years; Pinwheel had ~$8.5M cumulative revenue at its 2024 crowdfund; Gabb (the leader in kid-safe phones) is at roughly $105-149M revenue (unverified). Pitch the opportunity bottom-up, not with a TAM slide.

JioShield changes the Indian price anchor days before this brief. It launched 26-29 Sep 2026 at Rs 1,000/year (effectively free with the anniversary vouchers) for location, SOS, screen-time, app and contact control on any Android 10+ phone with a Jio number. Zune's unvalidated ~$13/month is ~Rs 1,250/month, which is about 15x JioShield's annual price and 5-6x an entire average mobile bill (Rs 215-264 ARPU). Zune only wins where parents value what a control layer cannot do: no browser, no YouTube, in-product contacts, AI and curated video.

The closest analogue already exists in the US. Pinwheel sells Pixel 9a phones running its no-browser kid OS at $599 plus $14.99/month, and Freckle (launched 1 Oct 2026) pitches a $199 'no browser, no app store, no YouTube' phone. This validates the concept and the Pixel choice, but means 'Pixel + no browser' is not a moat. Pinwheel's small funding (~$6.4M total) is also a caution about how much capital this category has attracted.

The regulatory tailwind in India is real and immediate but cuts both ways. On 28 Sep 2026 the Centre told the Supreme Court it will amend the IT Rules to bar under-18s from opening social accounts, and DPDP parental-consent duties bite from 13 May 2027. That builds demand for age-appropriate, parent-gated alternatives (the EU KIDS Act even carves out guardian-managed child video services, like Zune's Videos). But it targets platforms, so parents may conclude a normal phone becomes safe enough. The state bans (Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh) are announcements, not enforced law.

Premium India is real but iPhone-heavy, and Pixel is small. Counterpoint puts >INR 30k phones at 22% of 2025 units; IDC puts $600+ at ~10%. Apple holds ~65% of >INR 45k units (14M iPhones, 9% overall), and Samsung leads Android premium. Pixel was 2% of >INR 45k in 2025 and 4% in Q2 2026 (+68% YoY), helped by no price hikes while memory shortages pushed the market down 11% and the average price up 14%. Pixel 9a/10a at Rs 49,999 (~$519) fall in IDC's fastest-growing $400-600 band (8.6% share, +60%), which is a favourable band to be in. Over 50% of mainline phones are financed, which could also help finance the device.

Children's phone ownership in India is low and shared-device use dominates. Household smartphone access is 85.5% overall (MoSPI), but rural 14-16 year olds who own one are only ~31% (ASER 2024), and I found no India figure for ages 8-14. In the US and UK, own-phone rates jump at age 10-12 (Ofcom: 56% at 10, 83% at 11), which matches Zune's band. A Zune family in India is most likely buying a new, dedicated device for the child, not converting an existing child phone, which pushes the true cost to ~Rs 60-70k in year 1.

The ~200-user plan has a cold-start problem the market data hints at. The in-product messenger, voice, video and walkie-talkie only connect Zune kids with approved Zune contacts (D7/D8/D10/D19), while Indian children communicate over WhatsApp. Recruiting in clusters (same school, neighbourhood or parent group) matters more than raw count, and a Pixel-owner-only funnel scatters users across the country. Parent-side calling is deferred (D8), which weakens the pitch to parents who live apart from the child.

Pixel supply and service are a real operating risk, not just a market fact. Only ~3% of Pixel production is in India (2025), and the Pixel 11 launch price is 12.5% above the Pixel 10's. Walk-in service centres exist only in Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai. Because Zune flashes and re-locks customer phones, warranty, relock and stock questions (report 15) can limit which cities and phones are workable. I did not research those here.

Willingness-to-pay evidence is indirect and almost entirely foreign. US families pay $15-35/month for kid-phone services plus $120-300 for the phone, and about 71% of surveyed UK parents say they would pay operators for child controls (undated). In India the only direct anchors are JioShield (Rs 1,000/yr), kids watches (Rs 5,000-9,500), and free Family Link. The Rs 1,250/month idea matches a US price after currency conversion, not an Indian income level. Rupee weakness (Rs 96.3/$) also makes any USD-based pricing and Pixel cost more expensive for Indian buyers than a year ago.

Interest in a restrictive device is rising fast, but the cohort that already acts on it is small. About 155,000 US families have signed Wait Until 8th and a UK parent pledge counts 165,000-350,000 (sources conflict). 58% of countries now have a national school phone ban (UNESCO, up from 24% in 2023). For India, LocalCircles shows high parent concern (61% say 3+ hours/day; 73% back mandatory parental consent), but these are online self-selected panels and concern has not yet been shown to convert to purchases.
gaps: I could not open any source page. WebFetch returned EGRESS_BLOCKED for every domain I tried (fonearena, IDC, Counterpoint, Business World, TechCrunch, Pew, ASER, Bark, Gabb, Wikipedia), and a request to check the network proxy was denied by the permission system. Every figure here comes from WebSearch result summaries, so none of the IDC, Counterpoint, ASER, Pew, Ofcom or MoSPI primary documents was read in full. Please have a human re-verify the load-bearing numbers before external use: 152M units, 22% premium, 14% ultra-premium, Pixel 2% to 4%, 85.5% households, and JioShield pricing.

No published Pixel unit sales for India exist in what I found. My 0.3-0.5M per year and 1.6M cumulative figures are arithmetic on analyst shares, and two inputs are shaky: the 14% ultra-premium share (Q1 2025 only, and I am not sure it is a unit share) and the 'Pixel 5% in 2024' figure (ambiguous: all premium or Android premium). The fraction of Pixels that are 9a/10a (50-70%) is an assumption (the only data point is 73% in 2023).

The user's threshold (>INR 40,000, ~$415) is not reported by IDC (USD bands) or Counterpoint (>INR 30k, >INR 45k). I could only bracket it. Counterpoint's 'premium' definitions are inconsistent across the sources I saw: 20-22% of units for >INR 30k vs only 6.5M units in Q1-Q3 2024 for the 9to5Google 'premium' set that gives Apple 56%/Android 44%. Counterpoint's own total unit count for 2025 was not retrieved.

Q2 2026 Counterpoint arithmetic does not reconcile: Pixel +68% YoY with share doubling implies the >INR 45k segment shrank ~16%, yet Counterpoint calls it 'resilient'. IDC Q2 2026 shares for the $600-800 and $800+ bands were not retrieved. I estimated >$400 at ~19-20% of Q2 2026 units; this is not sourced.

No India data on children's phone ownership for ages 8-14, no urban-specific ownership by age, no count of households with a child 8-14, and no share of households that are English-medium (relevant to D20). ASER is rural and 14-16 only; McAfee is a vendor online panel on 'use', not ownership; LocalCircles is a self-selected online community.

No India-specific willingness-to-pay study for a kid-only device or subscription. WTP is inferred from price lists (JioShield, kids watches, Western plans). The UK ITPro survey (71% would pay operators) is undated in the excerpt and is about operator controls. Whether Rs 1,250/month is viable in India is untested. The '$59 + ~$13/month' pricing from earlier reports remains unvalidated.

India market value for parental-control software or kids phones: none found; only CAGR claims (13.3-13.7%) with no verified base. Kids-smartwatch India figures are corrupted or unusable. No India kids-smartwatch shipment numbers (IDC reports only total smartwatches).

Affluent household counts are weak. PRICE's '11M rich households' could not be opened or confirmed, and an 'NSE 46M households above Rs 10 lakh' figure appeared once and was not re-confirmed, so I excluded it. Goldman's 60M affluent counts individuals, not households. I did not find an urban household total.

Funding data comes from aggregators (PitchBook, Tracxn, Crunchbase, Dealroom, CB Insights, Latka) and is unaudited and sometimes contradictory. Gabb's $148.7M revenue (Latka, third-party) is unverified. Light Phone funding excluded (the listing mixed in another 'Light' company). Troomi's and Pinwheel's totals vary by source, and Pinwheel's current device and plan prices conflict between its site/Android Central ($119-599 + $14.99/mo) and TechCrunch (Jul 2026: $240 + $29/mo). 'Pinwheel' search results also mixed in an unrelated payroll company.

Aura/Qoria: the A$0.317 per share price and 'Aura 2026 data breach' mention came from excerpts. I used only the first. Qoria's stock reaction (-32/33%) is from Yahoo/Investing.com summaries. I did not verify the timeline between Qoria's Feb 2026 results, the Aura approach, and completion on 17 Jul 2026.

Very recent events could change: JioShield (26-29 Sep 2026), the Supreme Court hearing and the Centre's IT Rules statement (28 Sep 2026), the EU KIDS Act proposal (17 Sep 2026), Freckle's launch (1 Oct 2026). All are days to weeks old. Karnataka/Andhra bans are announcements; I found no notification or enforcement. I did not confirm JioShield terms (whether the vouchers make it free for all subscribers, iOS timing, SIM requirement) beyond news excerpts, nor JioBharat's current 2026 price.

Several tailwind items were not verified at source: UK Online Safety Act child-safety duties (25 Jul 2025) and Ofcom codes, Denmark/Spain/New Zealand status, UNESCO's 114-system count (taken from a UNESCO GEM page and Indian press summary), India's list of states with school phone bans, and 'Wait Until 8th' / Smartphone Free Childhood counts (sources conflict).

Out of scope or not researched but needed under D18: DoT/TRAI messaging and telephony rules, RBI recurring-payment (e-mandate) rules for the monthly fee, emergency-number handling, Pixel warranty and relock support in India, which Pixels support a custom AVB key (report 15), and Google/Play distribution risk. The exchange rate (Rs 96.3/$) is a snapshot and moves Pixel and USD-priced plans materially.
